How can being in the military affect my mental health?
If you were or are in the military, you may have experienced or witnessed a life-threatening event. You may have been on missions that exposed you to traumatic combat-related experiences, such as incoming fire, explosive devices, or dead bodies. Other military experiences, like military sexual trauma, can also affect mental health.
About 1 in 4 veterans of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan has been diagnosed with a mental health condition, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and anxiety.3 Left untreated, mental health issues can cause long-term problems for you, your family, and your community. Reach out to someone for help if you’re experiencing the signs of a mental health condition.
What is military sexual trauma?
Military sexual trauma (MST) is a term used by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to describe sexual assault or repeated, threatening sexual harassment that happens while the victim is in the military.4 MST can happen to both men and women, but female service members are at higher risk of MST. MST can also lead to depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and substance abuse. Studies show that 1 in 4 or 5 women in the military experiences MST.4,5
MST can happen during war, peace, or training. It can happen between people of the same sex or different sexes. If you’ve experienced MST, you may feel fear, shame, anger, embarrassment, or guilt. You may have trouble trusting people. You may even have physical symptoms like headaches, diarrhea, chronic fatigue, or gynecological problems.
When you’re actively serving, it can be difficult to report or talk about MST. The Department of Defense (DoD) has two ways (PDF, 329 K

records.title: mental-health_abuse-trauma-and-mental-health.txt
records.text:
headaches, diarrhea, chronic fatigue, or gynecological problems.
When you’re actively serving, it can be difficult to report or talk about MST. The Department of Defense (DoD) has two ways (PDF, 329 KB) for you to report assault if you are on active duty:
- Restricted reporting lets you confidentially report the assault to someone and get medical treatment and counseling, but it won’t trigger an actual investigation. This is intended to make it easier to report an assault and to give you time to heal mentally and physically. You can decide later if you want the military to begin a criminal investigation.
- Unrestricted reporting means that you will still receive medical treatment and counseling, but the assault will be reported through your chain of command. It will trigger an investigation.
If you have been assaulted or are unsure about what to do, you can call a confidential helpline that works specifically with the DoD community: the Safe Helpline. Call 877-995-5247, or visit safehelpline.org.
If you have experienced MST, you can also contact your nearest VA facility to speak with the MST coordinator. VA facilities have health care providers who are trained to treat the effects of MST. Many have specialized outpatient mental health services focusing on sexual trauma.
You may also be able to get compensation from the military to help with treatment (PDF, 168 KB).
How do I know if my mental health is affected by past abuse or trauma?
It can be difficult to tell whether or how much your mental health is affected by past abuse or trauma. Sometimes the symptoms of trauma or abuse don’t start to affect your life for many months or years after the event took place. If you have any of the following symptoms, talk to your doctor or nurse or reach out for help:
- Anxiety
- Tro

records.text:
buse don’t start to affect your life for many months or years after the event took place. If you have any of the following symptoms, talk to your doctor or nurse or reach out for help:
- Anxiety
- Trouble sleeping
- Anger
- Depression
- Changes in mood or appetite
- Abusing drugs or alcohol
What should I do if I’ve been abused or traumatized?
The sooner you can get professional help for abuse or trauma, the sooner you can begin to get better. If you have been physically hurt, visit a hospital or doctor right away. You may also need to call the police. The doctor and the police can help document what has happened to you. This documentation may be important later if you decide to press charges against someone who attacked you.
If you are experiencing changes in how you think, feel, or behave that are interfering with your ability to work or live your life normally, reach out to a mental health professional. Find a mental health professional near you. A mental health professional can help make sense of any symptoms you may be having that are related to your abuse or trauma. The professional can help you find the best kinds of treatment to help manage symptoms of the abuse or trauma.
If you’re in immediate danger, call 911.
You can also call helplines to talk about what happened to you or get guidance about what to do:
- National Domestic Violence Hotline
Phone Number: 1-800-799-SAFE (7233)
- National Sexual Assault Hotline
Phone Number: 1-800-656-HOPE (4673)
- Safe Helpline (for members of the military)
Phone Number: 1-877-995-5247
Abuse or trauma you have suffered is not your fault. You can get better with treatment.
How are abuse and trauma treated?
Symptoms caused by abuse or trauma can usually be treated with different types of talk therapy, medicine, or both. Therapy

How are abuse and trauma treated?
Symptoms caused by abuse or trauma can usually be treated with different types of talk therapy, medicine, or both. Therapy with a professional counselor can help you work through your feelings and learn healthy ways to cope. Medicines might include antidepressants or anti-anxiety medicine.
Today, complementary mind and body therapies, such as mindfulness and yoga, may be offered along with traditional treatments such as medicines and therapy.

Title: Body image and mental health | Office on Women's Health
Agency: HHS / Office on Women's Health
Licence: US federal public domain (17 USC 105)

Body image is how you think and feel about your body. Women with a positive body image are more likely to have good mental health. But many women in the United States have negative body images, which can put them at higher risk of depression, eating disorders, or other mental and physical health problems. You can take steps to develop a healthier body image and get treatment for mental health conditions.

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_how-do-i-know-whether-i-have-mental-health-condition.txt
records.text:
Source: https://womenshealth.gov/mental-health/good-mental-health/how-do-i-know-whether-i-have-mental-health-condition
Title: How do I know if I have a mental health condition?
Agency: HHS / Office on Women's Health
Licence: US federal public domain (17 USC 105)

Understanding what is considered "normal" mental health can be difficult. For example, when does nervousness become a phobia? When does "just feeling sad" become depression, which is a serious condition? A mental health professional can help you figure out whether you have a mental health condition. If you do, treatment can help you feel better. People can and do recover from mental health conditions.
How can I tell if I have a mental health condition?
If you’re experiencing a change in your thoughts, behaviors, or moods that is interfering with your work or relationships for longer than 2 weeks, you may have a mental health condition. It can be difficult to tell whether you have a mental health condition if you feel sadness, anxiety, or other intense emotions most of the time. Many mental health conditions first appear early in life, usually before 25 years old.
Symptoms of a mental health condition can include extreme anxiety most of the time, feelings of hopelessness about everything, or drug or alcohol abuse.
If you are in any doubt about your mental health, reach out to your doctor or nurse, a mental health professional, or a trusted loved one for help. If you have health insurance, this type of health care might be called “behavioral health” by your insurance plan. Many insurance plans call problems with drug or alcohol misuse “substance abuse” services.
Are mental health conditions really medical problems?
Yes. Mental health conditions are medical problems and can have just as big an effect on your life

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_how-do-i-know-whether-i-have-mental-health-condition.txt
records.text:
or alcohol misuse “substance abuse” services.
Are mental health conditions really medical problems?
Yes. Mental health conditions are medical problems and can have just as big an effect on your life as physical problems. Researchers know that the brains of people with mental health conditions often work differently from others. Some mental health conditions are related to higher or lower levels of certain brain chemicals. Events such as violence, abuse, and other traumatic experiences can make mental health conditions worse or more difficult to manage.
Many people with mental health conditions may be embarrassed to talk to a counselor or doctor or nurse about mental health or may think it’s a sign of weakness. But mental health conditions are health problems just like physical illnesses, and getting help when you need it is actually a sign of strength. If you are concerned about your mental health, do not hesitate to talk to someone or get help.
What are the symptoms of a mental health condition?
Talk to a mental health professional if you are experiencing:
- A lack of interest in things that you used to enjoy
- Crying spells
- Lack of motivation
- Inability to concentrate
- Significant changes in your eating or sleeping patterns
- An inability to cope with problems or daily activities
- More anxiety than usual over events or situations
- Feelings of hopelessness
- Sudden changes in your personality for no reason
- An inability to stop thinking about certain ideas or memories
- Sadness for longer than 2 weeks
- Thoughts about suicide (call 911 if you are in immediate danger)
- Drug or alcohol abuse or illegal use of prescription drugs
- Extreme mood swings
- Violent behavior or a lot of anger or hostility
- Hearing voices or seeing things that other people don’t hear o

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_how-do-i-know-whether-i-have-mental-health-condition.txt
records.text:
r)
- Drug or alcohol abuse or illegal use of prescription drugs
- Extreme mood swings
- Violent behavior or a lot of anger or hostility
- Hearing voices or seeing things that other people don’t hear or see
How are mental health conditions diagnosed?
There is no one test for mental health conditions. Your doctor, nurse, or a mental health professional may ask you about your symptoms and experiences and how long you’ve had them and talk with you about ways to deal with them.
How are mental health conditions treated?
Treatment for a mental health condition depends on the specific condition and how severe it is. Your doctor, nurse, or therapist may give you medicine, or your doctor or nurse may refer you for therapy, or do both. In very rare but serious cases when your life is in danger, such as a suicide attempt, you may need to stay at a hospital or other treatment facility.
There are also different types of therapy for different types of mental health conditions. For example, phobias (fears of specific things or situations that make a person avoid everyday activities) are treated differently from depression. Certain types of therapy can teach you skills to retrain how you think or act.
Other types of support that can help include building life skills (such as how to find a job or a place to live), learning how to manage your thoughts, eating healthy and exercising, finding a new community (such as a place of worship or a hobby group), and joining support groups.
Does mental health treatment work?
Yes, people can get better with treatment and other types of support. Different types of supports and treatments might work for different people. Try different types of treatment and support until you find what works for you. You may need to try different approaches at different

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_how-do-i-know-whether-i-have-mental-health-condition.txt
records.text:
types of supports and treatments might work for different people. Try different types of treatment and support until you find what works for you. You may need to try different approaches at different times in life.
How can I help make my treatment work?
If you have been diagnosed with a mental health condition, it’s important that you follow the advice of your mental health professional. You may need more than one treatment or a different treatment if your symptoms do not get better.
- Take your medicines as directed. Some medicines take time to work. Medicines may also have side effects. Work with your doctor or nurse to find the medicine that works best for you. Some people stop taking the medicine once they start feeling better, but this can be risky. Stopping a medicine very suddenly may cause serious side effects, including thoughts of suicide. Try not to stop taking medicine without talking to your doctor or nurse first. If you have concerns about your medicine, let your doctor or nurse know so you can work together to adjust the amount of medicine or find a different medicine.
- Participate fully in therapy. Therapy, sometimes called “talk therapy,” works best when you attend sessions as scheduled, are honest with yourself and your therapist, and do any “homework” between sessions.
- Reach out to friends and family or others for support. You are not alone. There are people who want to help you. If you are having thoughts about hurting yourself or someone else, Call or Text 988 the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline.
- Learn steps you can take to stay mentally healthy. Get enough sleep, make healthy eating choices, and get regular physical activity. Learn more steps you can take to support good mental health.
Will the medicine I take make me gain weight?
Maybe.

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_how-do-i-know-whether-i-have-mental-health-condition.txt
records.text:
thy. Get enough sleep, make healthy eating choices, and get regular physical activity. Learn more steps you can take to support good mental health.
Will the medicine I take make me gain weight?
Maybe. Some medicines that doctors prescribe for mental health conditions can make women more likely to gain weight than other types of medicine. This may be due to how your body processes the medicine. It may also be because getting treatment for a mental health condition can improve your appetite if you weren’t eating well before treatment.1
The most common medicines linked to weight gain are a type of medicine called antipsychotics, often used to treat schizophrenia (a serious mental health condition). Some antidepressants and mood stabilizers, which can be used to treat depression and bipolar disorder, can also increase the chances of gaining weight.2
All medicines have risks. Talk to your doctor or nurse about the benefits and risks of your medicines. If you’re concerned about gaining weight from your medicine, talk to your doctor or nurse about whether a different medicine or treatment method may work better.
How can I get help paying for mental health treatment?
Most health insurance plans cover mental health treatment in the same ways they cover medical or surgical treatments. There is not a different copay, coinsurance, or deductible for mental health treatment.
- If you have insurance, check with your insurance provider to find out what’s included in your plan. If you have insurance through your employer, you may be able to get help through an employee assistance program (EAP). Through your EAP, you may be able to get short-term counseling for stress, mental health symptoms, and substance abuse.
- If you have Medicaid, your plan will provide some mental health services.

records.text:
AP). Through your EAP, you may be able to get short-term counseling for stress, mental health symptoms, and substance abuse.
- If you have Medicaid, your plan will provide some mental health services. Some plans offer substance use disorder services.
- If you have Medicare, your plan may help cover mental health services, including hospital stays, visits to a therapist, and medicines you may need.
If you do not have insurance, use the mental health services locator on this page to find free or low-cost care on a sliding scale according to your income.

For more information about knowing whether you have a mental health condition, call the OWH Helpline at 1-800-994-9662 or check out the following resources from other organizations:

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_sleep-and-your-health.txt
records.text:
Source: https://womenshealth.gov/mental-health/good-mental-health/sleep-and-your-health
Title: Sleep and your health
Agency: HHS / Office on Women's Health
Licence: US federal public domain (17 USC 105)

Sleep affects your mental and physical health. Getting good sleep helps boost your mind and mood and can help prevent health problems. Women are more likely than men to have insomnia and other sleep problems.1 Changing hormones during the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and menopause can affect how well a woman sleeps. But there are steps you can take to get the rest you need.
How does sleep affect my mental health?
Your mind and body are healthier when you sleep well. Your body needs time every day to rest and heal. Some sleep disorders, such as insomnia, sleep apnea, and restless leg syndrome, make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep. This can lead to daytime sleepiness and make it more difficult to stay in good mental health.
Having a sleep problem can also trigger a mental health condition or make current mental health conditions worse. Also, mental health conditions or treatments can sometimes cause sleep problems.
What sleep problems affect women?
Sleep problems that affect women more or differently from men include:
- Insomnia. More than 1 in 4 women in the United States experience insomnia, or the inability to fall asleep or stay asleep.3 Insomnia is also more common in people with depression and anxiety, which also affect more women than men.4
- Restless leg syndrome. More women than men experience restless leg syndrome.5 It can happen to women of all ages, but it happens most often during pregnancy.6 Also, some medicines used to treat depression can cause restless leg syndrome. Depression is more likely to affect women compared to men.
- Sleep apnea. Sleep apn

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_sleep-and-your-health.txt
records.text:
happens most often during pregnancy.6 Also, some medicines used to treat depression can cause restless leg syndrome. Depression is more likely to affect women compared to men.
- Sleep apnea. Sleep apnea may be underdiagnosed in women. Snoring is one of the main signs of sleep apnea. Women with sleep apnea may be underdiagnosed, because they usually report more general symptoms, such as insomnia, anxiety, and nightmares.7
Why do women have more sleep problems?
Women may be more likely to have sleep problems because women experience hormonal changes during certain times and events that are unique to women. These include:
- Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Women with PMS commonly report trouble sleeping.8 Nearly 7 in 10 women with PMDD say they have problems going to sleep and staying asleep in the days leading up to their period.9
- Pregnancy, especially in the third trimester, when women may wake up more often than usual because of discomfort, leg cramps, or needing to use the bathroom.
- Perimenopause, when hot flashes and night sweats often can disturb sleep. Also, about half of women report problems sleeping after menopause.10
How do I know if I have a sleep disorder?
Talk to your doctor if:
- You often have difficulty sleeping and the sleeping tips are not working for you
- You awaken during the night gasping for breath
- Your partner says that your breathing stops when you are sleeping
- Your partner says that your legs move rapidly during sleep
- You snore loudly
- You have to get up more than twice during the night to urinate
- You wake up feeling like you haven’t slept or are exhausted
- You fall asleep often during the day
How are sleep disorders diagnosed?
To determine whether your sleep problems are caused by a sleep diso

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_sleep-and-your-health.txt
records.text:
ou wake up feeling like you haven’t slept or are exhausted
- You fall asleep often during the day
How are sleep disorders diagnosed?
To determine whether your sleep problems are caused by a sleep disorder or another mental or physical health problem, your doctor will ask you questions about your medical and sleep history. Sometimes it can take several visits to a doctor to figure out the cause of your sleep problems.
Your doctor or nurse may:
- Ask about any new or ongoing health problems or stress.
- Ask about your sleep habits. Consider keeping a sleep diary for 1 or 2 weeks before you see your doctor. Write down when you go to sleep, wake up, and take naps.11 Keep track of how long you sleep each night and you how feel throughout the day. Some free apps for your mobile phone may also help you track sleep.
- Do a physical exam. This can help your doctor rule out other medical problems that might cause sleep problems. You might need blood tests to check for thyroid problems or other health problems.
- Recommend a sleep study. If your doctor thinks a sleep disorder is causing your sleep problems, you may be asked to do a sleep study. Sleep studies may record brain activity, eye movements, heart rate, and breathing patterns while you stay overnight at a sleep center. A study can also record how much oxygen is in your blood and how much air moves through your nose while you breathe, as well as your snoring and other measurements.
Can I take an over-the-counter (OTC) medicine to help me sleep?
Yes, but talk to your doctor or nurse about your sleep problems before using an OTC product. Your sleep problem may be a symptom of a different medical problem that needs to be treated. Also, OTC products are not meant for regular or long-term use. If you decide to use a sleep medici

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_sleep-and-your-health.txt
records.text:
product. Your sleep problem may be a symptom of a different medical problem that needs to be treated. Also, OTC products are not meant for regular or long-term use. If you decide to use a sleep medicine, doctors recommend that you:
- Read the medicine label and directions first.
- Use the medicine at the time of day directed by your doctor or nurse.
- Do not drive or do activities that require you to be alert.
- Always take only the amount your doctor or nurse tells you to take.
- Tell your doctor or nurse about other medicines you use.
- Call your doctor or nurse right away if you have any problems while using the medicine.
- Do not drink alcohol or use drugs.
- Talk to your doctor or nurse if you want to stop using the sleep medicine. Some medicines must be stopped gradually.
What can I try at home to help me sleep better?
Try these tips to help improve your sleep:
- Try to go to sleep when you feel sleepy and then get up at the same time each morning.
- Do not take naps after 3 p.m. if you normally sleep at night.
- Do not drink caffeinated or alcoholic drinks or smoke late in the day or at night.
- Exercise on most days. Exercise or physical activity done too close to bedtime can make it harder to fall asleep. Experts recommend exercising at least 5 or 6 hours before your bedtime, especially if you have insomnia.
- Do not eat or drink a lot within about 3 hours of bedtime.
- Keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. If light is a problem, try a sleeping mask. If noise is a problem, try earplugs, a fan, or a “white noise” machine to cover up the sounds.
- Follow a routine to help relax and wind down before sleep, such as reading a book, listening to music, or taking a bath.
- If you cannot sleep within 20 minutes of going to bed or don’t feel drowsy, get out of bed. R

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_sleep-and-your-health.txt
records.text:
to help relax and wind down before sleep, such as reading a book, listening to music, or taking a bath.
- If you cannot sleep within 20 minutes of going to bed or don’t feel drowsy, get out of bed. Read or do a quiet activity until you feel sleepy. Then try going back to bed.
- Do not do anything in your bed that could make you more awake. Using a mobile phone, watching TV, or eating in bed can make it harder for you to fall asleep in bed.
- Do not look at lighted screens like a laptop or smartphone before bed.
- See your doctor or a sleep specialist if you think that you have a sleep problem.
How can I improve my sleep with a new baby?
Having a baby can make it a challenge to get enough sleep. It can take babies weeks or months to adjust to a sleeping routine or to start sleeping through the night. Also, changing hormone levels after giving birth can disrupt your sleep for a time. For some women, severe swings in hormone levels during and after pregnancy may cause a mental health condition called postpartum depression. Postpartum depression can also cause trouble sleeping.
If you have a new baby, here are some ways to get more rest or get help:
- Sleep when the baby is sleeping.
- Don’t try to do too much or to do everything by yourself. Ask your partner, family, and friends for help.
- Have a partner, a friend, or another caregiver help take care of your baby for a while so you can sleep.
- Talk with other mothers so that you can learn from their experiences.
- Join a support group for new mothers. Ask your doctor, nurse, or midwife about groups in your area.
- If you go back to work after childbirth, ask your employer if you can work part-time or reduced hours at first.
If you continue to have trouble sleeping, or if you think you are depressed, talk to your doctor,

records.title: mental-health_good-mental-health_sleep-and-your-health.txt
records.text:
back to work after childbirth, ask your employer if you can work part-time or reduced hours at first.
If you continue to have trouble sleeping, or if you think you are depressed, talk to your doctor, nurse, or midwife.

records.title: mental-health_living-mental-health-condition.txt
records.text:
Source: https://womenshealth.gov/mental-health/living-mental-health-condition
Title: Living with a mental health condition | Office on Women's Health
Agency: HHS / Office on Women's Health
Licence: US federal public domain (17 USC 105)

Women with mental health conditions face unique challenges. A mental health condition can make hormonal changes during your menstrual cycle and pregnancy worse. Some mental health conditions can make it harder to get pregnant. Living with a mental health condition also means knowing how to care for all aspects of your life. This includes knowing how you are protected under law at your job. You can learn ways to live well with and treat a mental health condition to lead a full life.

records.title: mental-health_mental-health-conditions_borderline-personality-disorder.txt
records.text:
Source: https://womenshealth.gov/mental-health/mental-health-conditions/borderline-personality-disorder
Title: Borderline personality disorder
Agency: HHS / Office on Women's Health
Licence: US federal public domain (17 USC 105)

Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious mental illness. It causes a person's moods, relationships, self-image, and behavior to be unstable from one day to the next. This can hurt family and work life, the ability to make long-term plans, and the person's sense of self-identity. Women are more likely than men to have BPD. Researchers are still learning about BPD, its causes, and its symptoms. There are treatments for BPD.
What is BPD?
BPD is a serious mental illness. It causes unpredictable or unstable moods and affects a person’s self-image and relationships.
What are the symptoms of BPD?
A person with BPD may experience intense times of anger, depression, and anxiety that may last only hours or, at most, a day. A person with BPD may also be aggressive, hurt themself, and abuse drugs or alcohol. Her self-identity, which may include long-term goals, career plans or jobs, friendships, relationships with loved ones, or values, is not stable over time and often changes.
A person with BPD may also have a history of intense and unstable relationships. Sometimes people with BPD view themselves or others as fundamentally bad or unworthy. They may feel misunderstood or mistreated, bored, or empty.
People with BPD are often impulsive. They may spend too much money, binge-eat, or have risky sex. People with BPD may have other mental health illnesses, including bipolar disorder, depression, anxiety disorders, substance abuse, and other personality disorders. People with BPD may also be more likely to harm themselves and die by suicide.
If you ar

records.title: mental-health_mental-health-conditions_borderline-personality-disorder.txt
records.text:
s, including bipolar disorder, depression, anxiety disorders, substance abuse, and other personality disorders. People with BPD may also be more likely to harm themselves and die by suicide.
If you are having thoughts about hurting yourself or someone else, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988, available for both Calls or Texts.
What causes BPD?
Researchers are not sure exactly what causes BPD. But certain factors can increase a person’s risk of BPD:2
- Family history. If you have a parent or sibling with BPD, you are more likely to develop BPD.
- Trauma. Many people with BPD have been through traumatic life events, especially childhood sexual abuse. Others have had unhealthy or abusive relationships. However, some people with BPD do not have a history of trauma, and many people who have experienced traumas do not have BPD.1
- Physical changes in the brain. Some people with BPD have physical changes in their brains, especially in areas that control impulsive behavior and emotions.
How is BPD diagnosed?
BPD can be difficult to diagnose. It often has symptoms that are the same as other mental health conditions. A mental health professional will ask about a person’s symptoms and personal and family medical histories, including any history of mental illnesses. It may take several doctor’s visits to diagnose BPD. There is no blood test that can show BPD.
How is BPD treated?
Therapy, or talk therapy, is the best treatment for BPD.3 A type of therapy called dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) specifically treats BPD.4 DBT involves talking one on one with a therapist, as well as with other people with BPD in a group setting. A team of therapists will also meet regularly to discuss treatment. DBT focuses on helping people with BPD to recognize and cont

records.title: mental-health_mental-health-conditions_borderline-personality-disorder.txt
records.text:
a therapist, as well as with other people with BPD in a group setting. A team of therapists will also meet regularly to discuss treatment. DBT focuses on helping people with BPD to recognize and control their emotions. The therapist helps the person feel accepted in their emotions and teaches new ways to behave.4 This type of talk therapy can help women with BPD learn to express themselves and their emotions in healthy ways and to pay more attention to changes in mood. Family members of someone with BPD may also benefit from talk therapy.
Sometimes medicine can help with some of the symptoms of BPD, such as mood swings, anxiety, or depression. Talk to your doctor or nurse about which medicines might be able to help your symptoms.

Title: Eating disorders | Office on Women's Health
Agency: HHS / Office on Women's Health

Eating disorders, such as anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder, are serious mental health conditions that can happen to anyone but are much more common in women. People with eating disorders eat too little or too much. Extreme eating or dieting is not a normal or healthy part of being a woman. Some eating disorders also involve people making themselves throw up or taking laxatives to get rid of the food, or extreme exercise to burn off the calories. All eating disorders are dangerous if left untreated.

records.title: mental-health_mental-health-conditions_obsessive-compulsive-disorder.txt
records.text:
Source: https://womenshealth.gov/mental-health/mental-health-conditions/obsessive-compulsive-disorder
Title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
Agency: HHS / Office on Women's Health
Licence: US federal public domain (17 USC 105)

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental health condition that makes a person have thoughts (obsessions) and rituals (compulsions) over and over that they cannot control or stop. People with OCD often also have anxiety and depression. OCD, like anxiety and depression, is treatable.
What is OCD?
OCD causes you to have the same thoughts (obsessions) and repeat the same behaviors (compulsions) over and over. Behaviors might include repeated handwashing, counting, constantly checking on a specific item (like whether the oven was left on), or cleaning. Sometimes the obsessions or compulsions are not logical or do not make sense. A person might have either obsessions or compulsions, but most people with OCD have both.
People with OCD repeat these rituals in the hope that their obsessive thoughts will stop. But the rituals give only short-term relief. Ignoring the urge to do the ritual makes people with OCD very anxious. Left untreated, obsessions and the need to perform rituals can take over a person’s life. Treatment can help.
What are the symptoms of OCD?
People with OCD often have intense, uncontrollable thoughts and behaviors. OCD symptoms can severely affect work or school, home life, and relationships.
Symptoms of OCD can include:1,2
- Fear of germs or contamination
- Unwanted or taboo thoughts about topics like sex, religion, or violence
- Aggressive thoughts toward others or yourself
- Excessive cleaning or handwashing, especially among women with OCD3
- Ordering and arranging things in a particular, precise way
- Repeatedly checking on th

records.title: mental-health_mental-health-conditions_obsessive-compulsive-disorder.txt
records.text:
essive thoughts toward others or yourself
- Excessive cleaning or handwashing, especially among women with OCD3
- Ordering and arranging things in a particular, precise way
- Repeatedly checking on things, such as whether the door is locked or whether the oven is off
- Compulsive counting
For someone with OCD, the thoughts (obsessions) and behaviors (compulsions) happen daily, often many times in one day.
What causes OCD?
No one knows what causes OCD. Researchers think that genetics and environment play a role. Researchers are also studying how changes in the structure of the brain in people with OCD might lead to the condition.4
Who is at risk of OCD?
About 1 in 100 Americans has been diagnosed with OCD. Half of people with OCD have a severe form of it.5 People with OCD are at higher risk of other mental health conditions, especially depression and anxiety.6 Eating disorders are more common in women with OCD.7
If your parent or sibling has OCD, you are more likely to have it too. Also, people who were abused during childhood are more likely to develop OCD. Some women with OCD report that their symptoms get worse during their menstrual cycle, during pregnancy, or after pregnancy when hormone levels change.8
What other health problems are linked to OCD?
- People with OCD sometimes have other mental health conditions, such as depression, eating disorders, substance abuse, or anxiety disorders. When a person also has other disorders, OCD is often difficult to diagnose and treat.
- A person can have symptoms of OCD together with or as part of other brain disorders, such as Tourette’s syndrome.
Getting the right diagnosis and treatment of other disorders is important to finding a treatment for OCD that works.
How is OCD diagnosed?
A mental health professional can diagnose OC

records.title: mental-health_mental-health-conditions_obsessive-compulsive-disorder.txt
records.text:
ette’s syndrome.
Getting the right diagnosis and treatment of other disorders is important to finding a treatment for OCD that works.
How is OCD diagnosed?
A mental health professional can diagnose OCD. She or he will talk to you about your symptoms, thoughts, and behaviors. The mental health professional will also ask about your family’s medical history.
OCD can sometimes be hard to diagnose, because its symptoms are like those of other mental health conditions, such as anxiety disorders. It is possible to have both OCD and other conditions. Not everyone who experiences obsessions or compulsions has OCD. To have OCD, the condition must cause significant mental or emotional distress and interfere with your ability to achieve everyday tasks at work, school, or home.
On average, most people with OCD are diagnosed by 19 years old. But girls are usually diagnosed later than boys.9
How is OCD treated?
Both behavioral therapy and medicine can help people with OCD. A type of behavioral therapy known as “exposure and response prevention” is often used to treat OCD. In this type of therapy, a person is exposed to whatever triggers the obsessive thoughts and then is taught how to stop doing the usual compulsive rituals, how to deal with the anxiety this causes, and how to stop obsessive thoughts.

records.title: 4. My Well-Being Toolkit.docx.txt
records.text:
My Well-Being Toolkit
"The good life is a process, not a state of being. It is a direction, not a destination." Carl Rogers
Understanding mental health through the lens of "me" and building a personal mental health vocabulary are important because they help you recognise how your personal experiences, culture, and background shape your perspective, leading to greater self-awareness and resilience. This self-understanding is crucial for managing your own well-being, improving relationships, and recognising that your individual experiences are not the universal standard. It also provides a foundation for addressing personal struggles, which can be a step toward seeking professional help when needed.
Benefits of Understanding Your Personal Lens
Increased self-awareness: Reflecting on how your unique experiences, culture, and background influence your worldview helps you understand your own reactions and thought processes. This self-reflection is a key component of mental health well-being.

Resilience: Developing resilience helps you adapt to challenges and bounce back from setbacks. By understanding how your personal history shapes your responses to stress, you can build stronger, more effective coping strategies and maintain your well-being even during difficult times.

Empowerment and validation: Identifying and understanding your own struggles can be a powerful process, especially when professional help isn't immediately accessible. It's a way to begin processing your own experiences, a necessary step on your mental health journey.

Greater kindness and openness: Acknowledging that you don't have a complete picture of the world or of those around you opens you to other viewpoints and makes you more compassionate towards yourself and others.

Better relationships: Under

records.title: 4. My Well-Being Toolkit.docx.txt
records.text:
ging that you don't have a complete picture of the world or of those around you opens you to other viewpoints and makes you more compassionate towards yourself and others.

Better relationships: Understanding your own "lens" improves how you interact with friends, family, and colleagues by helping you communicate your needs and understand their perspective more effectively.

Combating stigma: By understanding your own lens, you become better equipped to recognise and challenge the stigma surrounding mental health in society.
What is Wellbeing to ME
Well-being is a complex, multifaceted concept that explores what it truly means to be “me, myself, and I." It isn't solely about feeling good; it encompasses psychological, emotional, social, and physical states, all shaped by our individual uniqueness and the influence of our cultures and societies. Research shows that well-being can include feeling satisfied with life, having a sense of purpose, and cultivating positive relationships with others. When we talk about psychological well-being, it's about our mental health and how we function well in daily life, including traits like resilience and the ability to manage our emotions.
Everyone’s well-being language is different & that’s OK.
So, let’s take a second to really think about what well-being means to you personally, through your own “lens”. It’s not about ticking boxes or following some one-size-fits-all plan—it’s about figuring out what genuinely helps you feel balanced, fulfilled, and happy. Maybe it’s about making meaningful connections with others, or finding joy in little everyday moments, like a quiet walk, trying a new recipe, or heading out for a run. Take a moment to reflect on what you value most and the kind of life you want to lead. What makes you feel like

records.title: 4. My Well-Being Toolkit.docx.txt
records.text:
ttle everyday moments, like a quiet walk, trying a new recipe, or heading out for a run. Take a moment to reflect on what you value most and the kind of life you want to lead. What makes you feel like your best self? What makes you feel alive, confident, and at peace? The answers to these questions can help guide your journey toward a healthier, more fulfilling life.

What are My Values
"Our values are like fingerprints - nobody's are the same, but you leave 'em all over everything you do." Judith Beck
The things we care about most really reflect our values—they’re like gentle reminders guiding us, showing how we view the world and connect with others. Taking the time to truly understand our values isn’t just an academic exercise; it’s a way to foster personal growth and create a sense of inner peace.
When we pause and reflect on what truly matters in our lives, it not only gives us a clearer perspective on priorities but also helps us make more thoughtful decisions. This clarity can spark a renewed sense of confidence, purpose, and even belonging as we travel along our well-being journey. Embracing our values can enrich our lives and assist us in pursuing what we truly need to achieve mental well-being.
So, why not take this opportunity to dive a little deeper into the things that truly resonate with you? Pause for a moment to consider the core principles you believe in, the values that influence your actions, and the ambitions that inspire a sense of joy within you. By embarking on this journey of self-exploration, you’re not just dreaming—you’re creating a detailed roadmap for your life, filled with all the things that genuinely bring you joy and fulfilment.
And here’s the kicker, the more you align yourself with your core values, the easier it becomes to feel connec

records.title: 4. My Well-Being Toolkit.docx.txt
records.text:
ap for your life, filled with all the things that genuinely bring you joy and fulfilment.
And here’s the kicker, the more you align yourself with your core values, the easier it becomes to feel connected—not only to yourself but also to everything around you. You’ll find yourself feeling more grounded and in tune with your internal and external world, discovering that the little moments shine brighter when they are rooted in what matters.

My Needs
"Self-care is not selfish. You cannot serve from an empty vessel." Eleanor Brownn
Recognising the behaviours and/or activities that meet ‘My Needs’ is such an important step in looking after our mental well-being. Sometimes, we hold ourselves to impossibly high standards, and that can really affect how we view ourselves. Being honest with yourself and figuring out what you truly need can make a world of difference. After all, how we see ourselves often impacts our well-being more than how others see us.
It's perfectly normal to find yourself caught up in thoughts like, “I should have done better” or “I don’t deserve a break.” However, if we let these thoughts linger, they can really hold us back. Taking a little time to reflect on what you truly need—whether it’s a refreshing walk, cosying up with a great book, or just allowing yourself to zone out for a moment—can truly help you reset and feel more centred.
Self-care doesn’t need to be complicated or formal. It’s about simple, daily acts of self-compassion toward ourselves and others. Whether you’re facing a tough day or feeling a little off, taking time to care for your emotional, physical and/or mental health can lift your mood and help you face challenges more clearly. It also effectively reduces anxiety and stress, making you feel calm and upbeat.
Everyone’s journey is u

records.title: 4. My Well-Being Toolkit.docx.txt
records.text:
al, physical and/or mental health can lift your mood and help you face challenges more clearly. It also effectively reduces anxiety and stress, making you feel calm and upbeat.
Everyone’s journey is unique; no two are alike, and what brings joy to one may not to another. Consider this: if you put 100 people in a room and asked them something as simple as “What are your needs for overcoming a bad start to the day”, you'd get 100 varying responses. That's why exploring what truly clicks for you is vital—whether it's sharing laughter, enjoying hobbies, or taking a breather. The goal is to find small things that help you regain balance and remind you that you’re doing well, even on tough days.

Maintaining Me and My Well-being
‘It is an active process that connects the dots that connect our emotional, psychological, and physical health to get the most out of life.’
Maintaining our mental well-being is essential for our overall health, enabling us to build stronger relationships, boost self-esteem, and increase life satisfaction and resilience. Each person has core psychological needs, and there are specific ways to nurture these needs to sustain mental health. However, these methods can change depending on our current resources and circumstances. By recognizing and understanding what we need to support our mental well-being, we become better equipped to adapt to life’s challenges and maintain psychological stability. Psychology research highlights the importance of acknowledging individual differences in mental well-being, which helps us develop personalised strategies for self-care and continuous growth.

It is important to remember that setbacks may still occur, even when we are actively working towards improvement. Recognising these setbacks as part of the journey allows

records.title: 4. My Well-Being Toolkit.docx.txt
records.text:
-care and continuous growth.

It is important to remember that setbacks may still occur, even when we are actively working towards improvement. Recognising these setbacks as part of the journey allows us to approach them with compassion rather than frustration. By becoming attuned to our triggers and understanding how we might respond in less productive ways, we can make it easier to adjust our strategies, adhere to our plans, and seek support when needed. This proactive approach to mental health fosters resilience and encourages personal growth, ultimately leading to a more fulfilling life.
* Seven key domains: self (you), family, friends, work, health, finances, hobbies/social.

The Future
No plan survives first contact, but at least the direction is known.
Planning future aspirations, especially around identified challenges, can help us establish day-to-day activities while offering us meaning and purpose. It is helpful to think of these activities as a series of small steps. This makes it easier to manage and handle expectations. You can do something now with smaller steps rather than putting your goals and aspirations on hold.  Without a plan for the future, in the short or long term, we can feel lost and alone, which only perpetuates our negative cycles.

Having a structured plan is essential for independent work, especially when facing major challenges. Reflecting on completed tasks and anticipating possible obstacles are equally important, as they can influence the risk of relapse. While reviewing past work is necessary, it can become tedious without a clear goal—particularly after significant effort. The questions below are meant to guide these reviews by offering potential motivations, strategies for action, and ways to handle setbacks or relapses.

records.title: Burnout tool kit.docx.txt
records.text:
Burnout tool kit

This toolkit is designed to provide you with actionable steps to manage the symptoms of anxiety. It is based on Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT), an evidence-based approach recommended by the NHS and NICE. The goal is to help you understand and interrupt the "vicious cycle" of fear, catastrophic thinking, and physiological arousal that keeps anxiety active.

If you're feeling distressed, in a state of despair, suicidal or in need of emotional support, you can phone NHS 24 on 111. For an emergency ambulance, phone 999.

What is Burnout
Burnout is officially classified by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic, unmanaged stress, specifically in the workplace. While not classified as a formal mental health condition like depression, the syndrome is characterised by three core dimensions: a profound sense of energy depletion and exhaustion, a state of increased mental distance or cynicism related to one's duties, and a marked feeling of reduced professional efficacy or competence. It is crucial to acknowledge that this state of chronic exhaustion, detachment, and reduced effectiveness can be triggered by any prolonged, emotionally or physically draining demand, such as intensive caregiving, academic pressure, or high domestic responsibility, signalling a critical failure in the balance between demands and resources that requires strategic identification and dedicated recovery.

Burnout often creates a cognitive filter that reinforces feelings of failure and detachment. Recognising these automatic thoughts is the first step toward challenging them.

What Can Cause Burnout
Burnout is rarely caused by individual weakness; rather, it is the result of a prolonged mismatch between the individual and their envi

records.title: Burnout tool kit.docx.txt
records.text:
the first step toward challenging them.

What Can Cause Burnout
Burnout is rarely caused by individual weakness; rather, it is the result of a prolonged mismatch between the individual and their environment, often stemming from systemic or organisational factors. The primary causes typically include an excessive workload and pace that leaves no time for necessary recovery, reflection, or planning/organising; a fundamental lack of control or autonomy over how, when, or with whom tasks are completed; and insufficient reward or recognition for effort, which quickly depletes motivation and fosters cynicism. Further contributors are a breakdown of the community/social group due to toxic or unsupportive relationships, perceived unfairness in the distribution of tasks or compensation, and a serious conflict between personal values and organisational ethics.  Understanding these environmental and systemic factors is crucial because while burnout can look and feel like simple exhaustion or high stress, it is a fundamentally different physiological and emotional state that requires a unique, strategic approach to recovery.

Burnout is a chronic state resulting from an imbalance in which demands persistently outweigh available resources. The causes are typically rooted in environmental or systemic factors. Understanding these systemic and ecological factors is crucial because while burnout can look and feel like simple exhaustion or high stress, it is a fundamentally different physiological and emotional state that requires a unique, strategic approach to recovery.

Stress vs. Burnout
It is critical to distinguish between stress and burnout, as the strategies for treating them are different. Stress is typically characterised by over-engagement, where people feel they have too muc

records.title: Burnout tool kit.docx.txt
records.text:
t
It is critical to distinguish between stress and burnout, as the strategies for treating them are different. Stress is typically characterised by over-engagement, where people feel they have too much to do, and often presents with physical urgency (anxiety, hyperactivity); the primary emotion is fear that they will fail. In contrast, burnout is characterised by disengagement and depletion, where the emotional state is helplessness and the physical state is exhaustion; the core feeling is not that you will fail, but that your efforts are pointless. While stress requires better time management, burnout requires radical restoration and strategic re-engagement of depleted resources.

Part 1: Getting Started (Immediate Regulation)

When you feel overwhelmed by anxious emotions or a spiral of negative thoughts, your primary goal is to interrupt the cycle and reconnect with the present moment. This is Grounding & Distancing.

Feeling hyper, triggered and irritable is distressing. 'Grounding' techniques help you feel calmer and more present, balancing numbness and overwhelming emotions. They are key for creating mental space during stress. These techniques manage depressive rumination and anxiety by focusing on the present, interrupting the distress cycle. It involves shifting attention from overwhelming emotions to your immediate environment via your senses.

1. First Aid for High Arousal (Immediate Reboot)
When you're experiencing high fear, worry, or physical panic symptoms, use these techniques to signal safety to your nervous system and bring your awareness back to the present moment.
After grounding and feeling safe, take a moment to ask yourself the following questions.  If you answer ‘yes’ to any question, answer the follow-up question. 

Burnout Check-In: Identifying

records.title: Burnout tool kit.docx.txt
records.text:
nt moment.
After grounding and feeling safe, take a moment to ask yourself the following questions.  If you answer ‘yes’ to any question, answer the follow-up question. 

Burnout Check-In: Identifying Your Current State
This quick check is designed to help you pinpoint which dimension of burnout is most active right now. This is crucial because your recovery strategy must be tailored to the area that is most depleted.

Next Steps: Finding Your Focus
Based on your 'Yes' answers, you can prioritise your recovery actions:
If you answered YES mostly to 1 & 2 (Exhaustion): Your primary need is Restoration and Boundary Setting. You must immediately protect your sleep, nutrition, and downtime.
If you answered YES mostly to 3 & 4 (Detachment): Your primary need is Re-evaluating Social & Value Conflicts. You need to examine who or what is draining your emotional energy and establish clearer boundaries in your interactions.
If you answered YES mostly to 5 & 6 (Reduced Efficacy): Your primary need is Small Wins & Problem-Solving. You need to break down tasks into achievable steps to rebuild your sense of competence (Mastery) and challenge negative self-talk.

records.title: My Sustainability Path Toolkit - The Sustainability Model.docx.txt
records.text:
YOUR SUSTAINABILITY PATH TOOLKIT

The Self-Sustaining Path offers a structured approach to managing stress responses and building resilience effectively. It guides us through a process of self-habituation, enabling us to reduce our emotional and physiological reactivity to stressors gradually. By working through this model, we can learn to experience stress without being overwhelmed, ultimately transforming it into a source of motivation and personal growth.
To start using The Self-Sustaining Path, choose one or two challenges you're currently facing, including any related to completed toolkits, preferably beginning with those that cause the least stress. This method supports gradual implementation and boosts confidence as you move through the process. Remember, the Self-Sustaining Path is an ongoing journey, not a one-time event. Incorporate reflection breaks between stages to deepen understanding and integrate insights. Each tool in the Path can be used independently for daily problem-solving, reflection, and finding solutions. The model is flexible and can incorporate additional self-guided practices, including those from the toolkits, that fit your needs. For example, you might assess your current energy levels to use them effectively based on your tasks.
The process involves key stages: identifying problems and their daily impact; engaging in self-conceptualisation to see how issues influence thoughts and beliefs; recognising and challenging Thinking Errors, negative patterns that increase stress; using the H-CPR technique to evaluate your thoughts for helpfulness, positivity, and realism; understanding your Circles of Control to focus on actionable steps, reducing helplessness; and breaking challenges into Ladders to boost confidence and progress.
Consistently app

records.title: My Sustainability Path Toolkit - The Sustainability Model.docx.txt
records.text:
itivity, and realism; understanding your Circles of Control to focus on actionable steps, reducing helplessness; and breaking challenges into Ladders to boost confidence and progress.
Consistently applying The Self-Sustaining Path will help you develop self-awareness, reduce stress reactivity, enhance emotional regulation, improve problem-solving skills, increase confidence, and cultivate adaptive coping strategies.  Ultimately, this structured approach empowers you to transform your relationship with stress, turning it into a catalyst for personal growth and development.
Constructing our problem list
Everyone faces problems, often experiencing their effects without understanding their origins. Problems have specific meanings and functions, often with maladaptive characteristics.  Creating a problem list is essential as it aids us in identifying and clarifying difficulties that may not have been fully defined. In therapy, maintaining a structured list not only facilitates a deep understanding of the client's issues but also helps in establishing meaningful connections between these problems and their potential triggers and outcomes. By systematically categorising and reviewing problems, therapists can guide the therapeutic process more effectively and enhance treatment outcomes. Furthermore, research indicates that engaging clients in this process fosters a collaborative environment where clients can actively participate in their healing journey and gain insight into their patterns of behaviour, thereby fostering a more profound therapeutic alliance and ultimately leading to better recovery trajectories.
The first step is to identify the initial problem(s). Some may be able to understand and define their problem(s) and articulate them clearly, but are not able to make t

o better recovery trajectories.
The first step is to identify the initial problem(s). Some may be able to understand and define their problem(s) and articulate them clearly, but are not able to make the connection to the extent that this is impacting, such as:

However, it's very common to feel a general sense of unease or to only be able to identify initial thoughts, feelings, or behaviours that are symptoms of a deeper problem. For example, you might think or feel:

If you're having trouble pinpointing the exact problem, don't worry. These feelings and thoughts are important clues. To help you dig deeper and define your problems more clearly, consider these guiding questions for each area of concern:
What specific situation or event triggers this feeling/thought/behaviour? (e.g., "When I think about the presentation...")
What thoughts come to mind when this happens? (e.g., "I'm going to mess this up.")
What emotions do you feel in that moment? (e.g., "Fear, anxiety.")
What do you do (or not do) as a result of these thoughts and feelings? (e.g., "I procrastinate, I avoid preparing.")

Spend a few minutes thinking about and writing down the problems that brought you this toolkit (Annexe One – Problem List). For each problem identified, please also take a second to consider when your stress response is heightened, what you were doing then, how long it took to feel better, and what happened afterwards. This will help you see the patterns.
Where are my problems impacting
Next, evaluate the impact the issues are having on various aspects of your life, as detailed in the table below, and identify the corresponding life domain. Alternatively, consider moments when you feel most secure, what activities you engage in, and who accompanies you. Based on your insights into your ch

elow, and identify the corresponding life domain. Alternatively, consider moments when you feel most secure, what activities you engage in, and who accompanies you. Based on your insights into your challenges, this evaluation can be approached in two distinct ways.

The first is holistic, for those who have a more defined problem list and have a general sense of the overarching problem(s), like “I have a presentation coming up at work and it’s all I can think about, and I have become distracted, irritable and procrastinate” you can conduct a single impact score for each life domain.

It is valuable to reflect on the who, what, where, why, and when of stress responses, as these factors can reveal how issues affect different areas of life. When a stress response is activated, individuals may not always identify the exact cause of their feelings, but they can often recognize the situation that triggered them. Gaining this insight can be very helpful for developing and expanding a list of personal problems.

The second way is for those who are not able to fully define their problems, but are able to identify initial thoughts, some feelings or certain behaviours, such as ‘I can’t focus while working; I feel irritable when people offer help or advice; I’m so tired even though I sleep’.

Understanding the Ripple Effect: How Your Problems Impact Your Life
We all face challenges, and sometimes, it can feel like one problem creates a ripple effect, touching different parts of our lives. You've already done an amazing job by identifying your problem list and connecting them to different areas of your life (like work, relationships, or your personal well-being). You even scored them, which gives you a sense of how much each area might be affected.
Now, let's take a closer look at those problems. Instead of just listing them, we're going to "zoom in" an

records.text:
eing). You even scored them, which gives you a sense of how much each area might be affected.
Now, let's take a closer look at those problems. Instead of just listing them, we're going to "zoom in" and understand how they show up in your daily life and how you typically respond to them. This isn't about judgment; it's about gaining clarity, data for us to make informed decisions. Think of it like being a detective for your own well-being – asking gentle, curious questions to uncover the full picture.
In professional settings, therapists use a similar approach called "Socratic questioning." Don't worry, you don't need a degree in psychology to do this. It simply means asking yourself thoughtful questions to dig a little deeper. For example, instead of just saying "I'm worried," you might ask yourself: "What specifically am I worried about?" "What does this worry make me do or not do?" "How does this worry feel in my body?".  Below is a list of thoughtful questions to assist with reflection on the problem.

This process of expanding our problem lists (Annexe 3) isn't just about understanding the problem; it's a crucial step towards determining what you want to change. By seeing the full impact, you'll be better equipped to set meaningful goals and find ways to support yourself, promoting better mental health and preventing those small challenges from becoming bigger obstacles. This journey of understanding yourself is a vital part of building a stronger, more resilient you.

Before addressing these challenges, it’s essential to assess both the resources we have and those we lack. Without proper preparation, any setback can feel overwhelming and raise our stress levels. Evaluating our resources is like packing essentials for a hike—we need to know what tools, habits, and s

records.title: My Sustainability Path Toolkit - The Sustainability Model.docx.txt
records.text:
ack. Without proper preparation, any setback can feel overwhelming and raise our stress levels. Evaluating our resources is like packing essentials for a hike—we need to know what tools, habits, and support systems are in place, and what we still need, to ensure a successful well-being journey.
In every situation and at every level, we recognise the resources we have to handle external stressors and minimise disruptions. It's possible to experience stress without distress, which depends on how we view the resources available for managing these external pressures.
Stress = The perception that we have adequate resources (internally and externally) to manage external stressors.
Distress = The perception that we do not have adequate resources (internally and externally) to manage external stressors.

For instance, do we have emotional support in place, such as friends, family, or professional guidance? Do we have habits that nurture our physical health, like regular exercise or a balanced diet? Are there mental tools like resilience, mindfulness, or stress management techniques in our "well-being backpack"? Understanding these elements allows us to prepare thoughtfully, filling in the gaps before starting, so we are equipped to navigate our path toward holistic health and fulfilment.

In CBT, a therapist employs Cognitive Conceptualisation to identify clients’ core beliefs and behaviours. This process unveils how experiences influence perceptions of self, others, and the world, as well as coping strategies for negative beliefs. Core beliefs, rules, and assumptions affect emotions and actions, but understanding and predicting them can help start overcoming maladaptive pattern cycles.

A ‘Self-conceptualisation’ version (Annexe 4) in the self-sustaining model is shaped by CBT factors, influencing our thoughts and perceptions of ourselves.  Life events like work, relationships, and achievements can change this view, highlighting its flexible nature. It helps us recognise unhelpful cycles like catastrophizing and avoidance, enabling us to challenge negativity and act on our values, thus boosting resilience.

Establishing Core Beliefs
Now that we have identified our thinking patterns, it’s important to recognise the core beliefs that shape how we respond to situations. Core beliefs are deep-rooted perceptions of ourselves, often formed early in life, that guide our reactions to triggers and challenges. For example, believing “I am inadequate” can lead to the assumption “If I try, I will fail,” and the rule “I must avoid challenges.”

In cognitive therapy, we recognise that although these beliefs may feel deeply rooted, they are not immutable truths. To identify such beliefs, use the “Downward Arrow” technique (Annexe Five): start with a strong negative thought from the cognitive cycle in Annexe Four, and ask two key questions focused around - “If this is true, what does it [say OR mean] about me, others, or the world?” Keep questioning until you reach a core belief, usually beginning with “I am…” or “I will…”. Restructuring Negative Thoughts: Breaking the maladaptive cycles.
We have our self-conceptualisation and common thoughts that form the basis of how we see ourselves, others, and the world. However, it is vital to actively challenge and reconstruct negative thoughts rather than allowing them to operate unchecked. In cognitive therapy, unhelpful or distorted thinking patterns—often referred to as maladaptive thoughts or cognitive distortions—can reinforce negative emotions and unproductive behaviours, creating a self-perpetuating negative cycle sometimes called the ‘Default Network’ or maladaptive cycle.
Challenging thinking errors and maladaptive thoughts is essential, as unchecked patterns can negatively impact self-esteem, relationships, and decision-making, often resulting in anxiety, low mood, or avoidance. Cognitive therapy stresses the importance of identifying, questioning, and restructuring these automatic negative thoughts to disrupt the cycle and foster a more balanced, compassionate self-view. By regularly confronting these thoughts, we gain insight into the core beliefs driving our responses, enabling us to adopt more adaptive ways of thinking. Over time, thi

nced, compassionate self-view. By regularly confronting these thoughts, we gain insight into the core beliefs driving our responses, enabling us to adopt more adaptive ways of thinking. Over time, this process becomes second nature, enhancing our confidence, emotional stability, and overall resilience. Ultimately, restructuring negative thoughts is a transformative and practical tool at the heart of cognitive therapy and personal growth.
Challenging Negative Thoughts – The HCPR Approach
Restructuring negative thoughts is essential for encouraging positive change. The H-CPR model offers a practical way to assess a single negative thought by examining its Helpfulness, Constructiveness, Positivity, and Reflectiveness in Reality. While some thinking aspects may be realistic and helpful, others might be irrational, negative, and unproductive. Clinging to unrealistic and negative beliefs about ourselves and our experiences can lead to emotional distress and potentially contribute to emotional disorders if left unaddressed.

For each aspect (Helpfulness, Constructiveness, Positivity, Reflectiveness in Reality), write a brief self-reflection. Consult Annexe Six A for an example to guide you through the process.
Challenging Thinking Errors (Cognitive Distortions)
Once we identify and record our thinking errors in Annexe Four, we can start challenging them in Annexe Seven. By monitoring and evaluating our thoughts, we learn to respond more adaptively. Common thinking errors, such as catastrophising or all-or-nothing thinking, are automatic patterns that can distort our perception and affect our behaviour. These habits aren’t cha

nd more adaptively. Common thinking errors, such as catastrophising or all-or-nothing thinking, are automatic patterns that can distort our perception and affect our behaviour. These habits aren’t character flaws, but ways our minds try to protect our core beliefs.
The good news is that with consistent practice, we can rewire our brains for more balanced and realistic thinking—much like building strength through repeated exercise. Over time, these new thought patterns become more natural and automatic.
Circles of Control
It is quite common, especially when we are triggered by a challenging situation, to fixate on aspects that are beyond our control. While this may feel like a protective strategy—believing that by focusing on the uncontrollable, we can prepare for any outcome—in reality, this approach is misleading.
Dwelling on what we cannot control is often linked to thinking errors or cognitive distortions, and it can lead to self-fulfilling prophecies, where our actions unconsciously shape negative outcomes. The Circles of Control model encourages us to redirect our focus towards what we can genuinely control: our own thoughts, actions, and reactions. By doing so, we empower ourselves to take constructive steps forward, rather than becoming stuck in worry or avoidance. There are also areas we can influence—such as our relationships or certain circumstances—but not fully control.
Completing the Circles of Control worksheet (Annexe Eight), based on your earlier self-reflection and thought-challenging exercises, will help clarify where to direct your energy for the greatest positive impact. Taking Action: Goal Setting
Setting a meaningful goal (Annexe Nine) is valuable, as it offers a sense of direction and a foundation for personal growth. Overcoming challenges and reaching your objectives is viewed as a gradual journey, involving a series of manageable steps that address your unique needs. Rather than becoming overwhelmed by the perceived distance to the end goal, it can be helpful to focus on the immediate step before you. Creating a visual map of these steps, as suggested in Annexe Nine, can bring reassurance and a sense of progress. When you encounter steps that appear daunting or ambiguous, use the SMART model to break them down into achievable, relevant actions tailored to your circumstances. There is no need to label every step in advance—begin by identifying and highlighting the first few practical actions, as these mark the beginning of your journey. As you start taking these steps, further actions will naturally become clearer. For example, if your goal is to manage anxiety in order to deliver a presentation, relevant steps might include practising relaxation techniques, gradually increasing exposure to speaking situations, preparing and rehearsing your presentation, and seeking feedback or support as needed. Each step should reflect your own experience, integrating different therapeutic strategies as practised across various toolkits to best support your progress.

A cost-benefit analysis involves systematically evaluating the advantages and disadvantages of a specific decision, behavior, or goal. By outlining both short- and long-term costs and benefits, practitioners can make well-informed decisions to address key challenges effectively. This process helps in understanding the overall situation and determining whether the necessary resources are available to mitigate potential negative effects while working toward desired outcomes.
To promote personal growth and well-being, it is crucial to identify and analyse the impact of life's challenges across various domains. Select one or two significant challenges, goals, or behaviours you wish to change, and consider them within the context of the specific life domains they affect. Ask yourself, “What is the cost of addressing these issues and taking action… versus what is the cost of not doing so?”

Problem identification:
Everyone faces problems, often experiencing their effects without understanding their origins.  However, in the case of ShiftedAI, this will not be the case as the user shall be selecting the bot - difficult conversation, etc., based on their initial problem.
Problems have specific meanings and functions, often with maladaptive characteristics.  Creating a problem list is essential because it helps us identify and clarify difficulties that may not have been fully defined. In therapy, maintaining a structured list not only facilitates a deep understanding of the client's issues but also helps in establishing meaningful connections between these problems and their potential triggers and outcomes. By systematically categorising and reviewing problems, therapists can guide the therapeutic process more effectively and enhance treatment outcomes.
The first step is to identify the initial problem(s). Some may be able to understand and define their problem(s) and articulate them clearly, when outlining the situation that brought them to ShiftedAI, but are not able to make the connection to the extent that this is impacting, such as:

However, it's very common to feel a general sense of unease or to only identify initial thoughts, feelings, or behaviours that are symptoms of a deeper problem. For example, you might think or feel:

If you're having trouble pinpointing the exact problem, don't worry. These feelings and thoughts are important clues. To help you dig deeper and define your problems more clearly, consider these guiding questions for each area of concern:
·       What specific situation or event triggers this feeling/thought/behaviour? (e.g., "When I think about the presentation...")

Prioritising well-being is essential for health, relationships, self-esteem, and satisfaction. Our needs, influenced by mood and stress, guide our well-being. Understanding our ‘Well-Being Language’ helps manage shifts and sustain positive cycles. Thoughts, emotions, and behaviours are interconnected, affecting mental health, as illustrated by the cognitive cycle responses to stress.

In CBT, a therapist employs Conceptualisation to identify clients’ Strength Beliefs (Negative Thoughts; Thinking Errors) and Responses (Feeling/Emotions; Behaviours) which are influenced by a person's rules, assumptions and intermittent beliefs. This process reveals how previous experiences shape perceptions of self, others, and the world, as well as coping strategies for addressing negative beliefs. A conceptualisation is a model that is used to construct key factors which will contribute to and influence how we respond in a given situation. Life events such as work, relationships, and achievements can change this view, highlighting its flexibility. It helps us recognise unhelpful cycles such as catastrophising and avoidance, enabling us to challenge negativity and act on our values, thereby boosting resilience.

During the conceptualisation phase, we aim to gather key information on the following areas.

Situation -> Triggers - > Strength of Belief -> Strength of Response.

When creating this conceptualisation, it's not crucial to scrutinise each phase individually. Usually, when eliciting the situation, triggers, thoughts, feelings, and behaviours will be provided, which should then be integrated into the model. Follow-up questions can help expand or clarify these aspects.
The Situation (The "What")
A situation is an objective, neutral, or stressful event. It is a fact that could be observed by anyone, such as:
Receiving an email from a boss.
Sitting in traffic.
A friend is not answering a text immediately.
Being in a crowded room.
In therapy, a situation is merely the setting or the event that triggers a thought, but it is not inherently "charged" for everyone.

The Trigger (The "Why")
A trigger is a stimulus—such as a sight, sound, smell, person, or a specific thought—that elicits a strong, often disproportionate, reaction. It acts as a "bridge" to a past painful experience, making the present feel unsafe.

Unique to the Individual: What triggers
